1) Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis (LWNH) / pigmentary mosaicism — Most likely. Childhood onset, hyperpigmented macules in Blaschko distribution, slow progression, asymptomatic, biopsy: increased basal pigmentation with normal melanocyte number and minimal inflammation — classic pattern.

2) Pigmented linear (blaschkoid) epidermal nevus — Possible but less likely. Clinical distribution fits, but epidermal nevi usually show epidermal hyperplasia/papillomatosis on histology, which is absent here.

3) Segmental (linear) Becker nevus — Less likely. Typically appears around puberty, often with hypertrichosis and epidermal change; histology and clinical timing do not favor it.

4) Lichen planus pigmentosus / post‑inflammatory hyperpigmentation — Unlikely. These usually have a history of inflammation or lichenoid/interface changes on histology, which are absent.

5) Pigmentary mosaicism associated with a genetic/congenital syndrome (e.g., blaschkoid manifestations of mosaic gene disorders) — Possible but less specific; consider if any extracutaneous anomalies present.

Recommendation: LWNH/pigmentary mosaicism is the leading diagnosis. If concerned about associated systemic findings, perform targeted review of systems (neurologic, developmental, musculoskeletal, ocular, dental) and consider dermatology follow-up for clinical confirmation and genetic evaluation if extracutaneous signs are present.
